lessonTitle: Frequency Response: Gain, Phase and Bandwidth of a First-Order System

blocks.text: A hydraulic test rig is commanded to move a specimen sinusoidally, 2 mm in amplitude, and the engineer raises the command frequency step by step. At 1 Hz the piston follows almost perfectly. At 10 Hz it moves only half as far and arrives about one-sixth of a cycle ($60^\circ$) late, as a first-order lag would give. Frequency response is the tool that predicts exactly how much the amplitude shrinks and how far the phase lags at every frequency.

blocks.markdown: If a stable linear system with transfer function $G(s)$ is driven by $u(t)=A\sin\omega t$, then after the transient dies out the output is a sinusoid of the **same frequency**: $y_{ss}(t)=A\,|G(j\omega)|\sin\big(\omega t+\angle G(j\omega)\big)$. The complex number $G(j\omega)$, obtained by substituting $s=j\omega$ with $\omega$ in rad/s, therefore gives the amplitude ratio and phase shift directly. This holds only for stable systems, because for an unstable one the transient never decays.

blocks.title: Frequency response
blocks.text: The frequency response of $G(s)$ is $G(j\omega)$. Its magnitude $|G(j\omega)|$ is the ratio of output amplitude to input amplitude in steady state; its argument $\angle G(j\omega)$ is the phase of the output relative to the input (negative means the output lags). Frequency in Hz is $f=\omega/2\pi$.

blocks.markdown: **First-order system.** For $G(s)=\dfrac{K}{\tau s+1}$ we have $G(j\omega)=\dfrac{K}{1+j\omega\tau}$. Rationalising, the magnitude is $K/\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^2}$ and the phase is $-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)$. At low frequency ($\omega\tau\ll1$) the system passes the input with gain $K$ and almost no lag; at high frequency ($\omega\tau\gg1$) the amplitude falls as $1/\omega$ and the lag approaches $90^\circ$. The transition happens near $\omega=1/\tau$.

blocks.caption: Steady-state amplitude ratio and phase of a first-order lag ($\omega$ in rad/s, $\tau$ in s).

blocks.title: Amplitude and phase of the output
blocks.prompt: A first-order sensor with $K=3$ and $\tau=0.05$ s is driven by $u(t)=2\sin(30t)$ (30 rad/s). Find the steady-state output.

steps.text: Output amplitude is input amplitude times gain: $2\times1.664=3.328$.

blocks.answer: $y_{ss}(t)=3.33\sin(30t-56.3^\circ)$: amplitude 3.33 and a lag of $56.3^\circ$ (equivalent to a time delay of $0.98/30=0.033$ s).

blocks.title: Corner frequency and bandwidth
blocks.text: The **corner (break) frequency** of $K/(\tau s+1)$ is $\omega_c=1/\tau$ rad/s, equivalently $f_c=1/(2\pi\tau)$ Hz. There the gain is $K/\sqrt2$ (down 3.01 dB) and the phase is $-45^\circ$. The **bandwidth** $\omega_b$ is the frequency up to which the system passes inputs with gain within 3 dB of its low-frequency value; for a first-order system $\omega_b=\omega_c=1/\tau$.

blocks.caption: Frequency response of a first-order lag normalised by its corner frequency

blocks.markdown: **Bandwidth and speed of response.** A system with a wide bandwidth can follow rapidly varying inputs, so it also reacts quickly to steps. For the first-order case $\omega_b=1/\tau$, so the 10-90% rise time $t_r=\tau\ln9\approx2.2\tau=2.2/\omega_b$. In hertz, $t_r\approx0.35/f_b$. Doubling the bandwidth halves every time scale. The price is that a wide-bandwidth system also passes more high-frequency measurement noise.

blocks.title: Corner, bandwidth and rise time
blocks.prompt: A sensor has transfer function $G(s)=\dfrac{40}{s+8}$ ($s$ in rad/s). Find its DC gain, corner frequency in rad/s and Hz, time constant, and the 10-90% rise time.

steps.text: Put the transfer function in time-constant form by dividing top and bottom by 8: $G(s)=\dfrac{5}{0.125s+1}$.
Read off $K=5$ and $\tau=0.125$ s. The corner frequency is $1/\tau=8$ rad/s.

blocks.answer: $K=5$, $\tau=0.125$ s, $\omega_c=\omega_b=8$ rad/s ($1.27$ Hz), 10-90% rise time $0.275$ s. At 8 rad/s the gain is $5/\sqrt2=3.54$.

items: Replace $s$ by $j\omega$ and write $G(j\omega)$ in the form $K/(1+j\omega\tau)$.
Compute $\omega\tau$ with $\omega$ in rad/s (convert from Hz with $\omega=2\pi f$).
Output amplitude is the input amplitude times the magnitude; the output is shifted by the phase.
Locate $\omega_c=1/\tau$ and use it to judge bandwidth and speed of response.

blocks.title: Common slips
blocks.text: Using hertz where rad/s is required is the most common error: $\omega=2\pi f$. The frequency response describes the steady-state response only, and the phase is for the sinusoidal output relative to the input, not a delay in seconds (the time delay is $|\phi|/\omega$ with $\phi$ in radians). Do not use the -3 dB point of the DC gain as $K/2$: the amplitude is $0.707K$.

blocks.title: Bandwidth is speed
blocks.text: For a first-order system corner frequency, bandwidth and $1/\tau$ are the same number. Larger bandwidth means smaller time constant, shorter rise time, and also more noise passed. When you need to compare sensors or actuators, compare $\omega_b$ or $f_b$.

points: For a stable system and input $A\sin\omega t$, the steady-state output is $A|G(j\omega)|\sin(\omega t+\angle G(j\omega))$.
A first-order lag has magnitude $K/\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^2}$ and phase $-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)$.
The corner frequency is $1/\tau$ rad/s ($1/(2\pi\tau)$ Hz); there the gain is 0.707 of DC and the phase is $-45^\circ$.
Bandwidth is inversely proportional to the time constant, and the 10-90% rise time is $2.2/\omega_b$.

questions.stem: A first-order positioning stage has transfer function $G(s)=\dfrac{2}{0.2s+1}$ (dimensionless gain, $\tau$ in s). A sinusoidal command $5\sin(10t)$ mm is applied, where $t$ is in s. Find the steady-state amplitude of the output in mm.
questions.explanation: With $\omega=10$ rad/s and $\tau=0.2$ s, $\omega\tau=2$. The gain is $2/\sqrt{1+4}=0.894$, so the output amplitude is $5\times0.894=4.47$ mm. The result is valid in steady state because the pole at $-5$ rad/s is stable.

questions.stem: A pressure transducer behaves as $G(s)=\dfrac{10}{0.01s+1}$. A pressure oscillation at 150 rad/s is applied. Find the steady-state phase shift of the output relative to the input in degrees (give a negative number for a lag).
questions.explanation: The product $\omega\tau=150\times0.01=1.5$. The phase is $-\tan^{-1}(1.5)=-56.3^\circ$, a lag, because the output of a first-order lag always trails the input. The magnitude at this frequency would be $10/\sqrt{3.25}=5.55$.

questions.stem: A sensor is modelled as $G(s)=\dfrac{25}{s+40}$ with $s$ in rad/s. What is its corner frequency?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the pole is at $s=-40$, so $\omega_c=40$ rad/s and $f_c=40/2\pi=6.37$ Hz.
distractorRationale.b: The numerator 25 is part of the DC gain $25/40$; it does not set the corner.
distractorRationale.c: The units are mixed up: 40 is in rad/s, not Hz.
distractorRationale.d: This is the DC gain $25/40$, not a frequency.

questions.explanation: In time-constant form $G(s)=0.625/(0.025s+1)$, so $\tau=0.025$ s and $\omega_c=1/\tau=40$ rad/s. Converting to hertz divides by $2\pi$ to give 6.37 Hz.

questions.stem: A first-order system has DC gain 1 and is driven at exactly its corner frequency, $\omega=1/\tau$. Which pair gives the steady-state amplitude ratio and phase?

distractorRationale.b: The amplitude is $1/\sqrt2$, not 1/2: the 3 dB point is not the half-amplitude point.
distractorRationale.c: $-90^\circ$ is the high-frequency limit; at the corner the phase is half that.
distractorRationale.d: A first-order lag always attenuates at the corner; unit gain applies only at low frequency.

questions.explanation: At $\omega\tau=1$ the magnitude is $1/\sqrt2=0.707$ (down 3.01 dB) and the phase is $-45^\circ$. These two values define the corner frequency in practice.

questions.stem: A first-order system has time constant $\tau$. By how many decibels is the steady-state gain below its DC value when it is driven at $\omega=10/\tau$?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $-10\log_{10}(1+100)=-20.04$ dB, essentially one decade of roll-off at $-20$ dB/dec.
distractorRationale.b: That is the loss at the corner, $\omega=1/\tau$.
distractorRationale.c: This uses the wrong decibel formula or counts half a decade.
distractorRationale.d: $-40$ dB per decade is the slope of a second-order system, not first order.

questions.explanation: The magnitude is $1/\sqrt{1+100}=0.0995$, which is $20\log_{10}0.0995=-20.04$ dB. A decade above the corner a first-order lag falls at $-20$ dB per decade.

questions.stem: A fast-response temperature probe is specified as first-order with a bandwidth (the -3 dB frequency) of 4 Hz. Estimate its 10-90 percent step-response rise time in seconds, using $t_r=\tau\ln 9$ where $\tau=1/(2\pi f_b)$.
questions.explanation: The time constant is $\tau=1/(2\pi\times4)=0.0398$ s. The rise time is $\tau\ln9=0.0398\times2.197=0.0874$ s, which agrees with the rule of thumb $0.35/f_b=0.0875$ s.

questions.stem: Sensor A has a bandwidth of 2 Hz and sensor B has a bandwidth of 8 Hz. Both are first-order. Which statement about their step responses is correct?

options.text: B has a time constant four times smaller than A
B has a time constant four times larger than A
B has a time constant equal to A but a higher gain
Bandwidth does not affect the step response

questions.correctOptionText: B has a time constant four times smaller than A

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $\tau=1/(2\pi f_b)$, so quadrupling the bandwidth divides $\tau$ by four.
distractorRationale.b: The relation is inverse: a larger bandwidth means a smaller time constant.
distractorRationale.c: Gain and bandwidth are independent; the question concerns speed, and speed follows from $\tau$.
distractorRationale.d: Bandwidth and rise time are directly related, $t_r\approx0.35/f_b$.

questions.explanation: For a first-order system bandwidth and time constant are reciprocal, $\tau=1/\omega_b$. B therefore has $\tau_B=\tau_A/4$ and a rise time four times shorter, so it tracks fast changes better but also passes more noise.

questions.stem: When a stable first-order system is driven by a steady sinusoid, the steady-state output has a different frequency from the input, because the system attenuates the amplitude.
questions.explanation: A linear time-invariant system cannot create new frequencies. The steady-state output has the same frequency as the input, with a changed amplitude and phase given by $|G(j\omega)|$ and $\angle G(j\omega)$.

questions.stem: Derive the steady-state amplitude ratio and phase of $G(s)=K/(\tau s+1)$ for a sinusoidal input $A\sin\omega t$. State how the result changes for $\omega\tau\ll1$ and $\omega\tau\gg1$, and give the corner frequency in rad/s.
markingGuide: Output has same frequency; amplitude is $A|G|$ with the phase added
Low frequency: gain about $K$, lag about $0^\circ$; high frequency: gain falls like $K/(\omega\tau)$, lag tends to $-90^\circ$
Corner frequency $1/\tau$ rad/s with gain $0.707K$ and phase $-45^\circ$
questions.explanation: The derivation follows from rationalising the complex gain. A good answer ties the corner frequency to the pole location $-1/\tau$.

questions.stem: Two linear actuators have first-order dynamics with the same DC gain. Actuator X has a corner frequency of 3 Hz and actuator Y has 12 Hz. Compare their time constants, rise times and ability to follow a 5 Hz sinusoidal command, and give one disadvantage of the larger bandwidth.
markingGuide: Computes $\tau=1/(2\pi f_c)$: X about $0.053$ s and Y about $0.013$ s (Y four times faster)
Rise time $\approx0.35/f_b$: X about $0.117$ s, Y about $0.029$ s
At 5 Hz X has $\omega\tau=5/3=1.67$, gain about $0.51$, phase about $-59^\circ$; Y has $5/12=0.42$, gain about $0.92$, phase about $-22.6^\circ$
Concludes Y tracks the 5 Hz command much better
States that a wider bandwidth passes more high-frequency noise or demands more actuator effort
questions.explanation: Because $\omega\tau=f/f_c$ for a first-order lag, frequency ratios are all that is needed for the gain and phase. The gains are $1/\sqrt{1+1.667^2}=0.51$ and $1/\sqrt{1+0.4167^2}=0.92$, which shows why bandwidth is the natural measure of speed.
